1.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings are set BACK from the top of the route, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down to the lower anchor at the base of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's LEFT of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
1.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the RIGHT side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.

2.station: Toss the rope slightly LEFT of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft ABOVE the anchor at the top of the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them

3.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it

4.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-LEFT one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below

5.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You CANNOT see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; it is still described as 'we will flag this tree soon' years later
5.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.

6.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at either of the anchors at the top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook

7.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor

8.station: Final rappel to the base of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and quite exposed.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
8.pull: Consider staying on rappel and walking back to the belay bolt at the start of the route, then pulling the rope from there.

set.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a SINGLE 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60, and the eight-station description dates from then. Accounts written before that assume a single 70 m or two 60 m ropes, and counts from that era differ honestly - eight single-rope rappels on a 70, or seven - so an older report disagreeing with this table is describing the pre-2019 descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's LEFT of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are published for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures on file are nominal rather than measured.

1.station: Rappel the climbing line down to the point where the descent leaves it - the bottom of pitch 8 in the route page's current 8-pitch numbering, which older beta and every trip report call the bottom of pitch 6 (the same place; the count differs by whether the traverse pitches are numbered). A 70 m rope links the two rappels above it into one full-stretch 35 m shot and skips the semi-hanging belay; a 60 m needs both stations.
hazards: One party who rappelled from the true top judged there were too many places for the rope to hang up to risk pulling it in one go from here

2.station: The rappel route leaves the climb here and this is the station people get wrong. From the anchor, go climber's RIGHT along the base of the wall, following a ramp and hugging the wall for about 30 m - not straight down. The published test is blunt: if your body is not touching the wall, you are not far right enough. The anchor is in a narrow gully on the far climber's right, under a small tree.
hazards: Rappelling the fall line instead of traversing right lands you on the wrong ground; multiple parties report going too far left here and having to swing back
One party went so far wrong they considered simul-rappelling because the rock they were on looked very loose

3.station: This one is straight down the fall line, close to a full-length rappel. Look for the anchor to climber's LEFT as you come down.
hazards: Having been told to go hard right on the rappel above, parties overcorrect and go too far right on this one

4.station: The hidden anchor, and the one the route page itself flags. It is NOT straight down: go climber's right over a slight rib into the next gully. Look over the rocky spine for a blue-green gully; the station sits beneath a band of blue-green rock forming the gully wall. There is a big tree down and to the LEFT with a sling on it - that is the wrong gully and the wrong anchor.
hazards: This is the station named in the route description as somewhat hidden, and the tree anchor to its left is an active decoy that parties have rappelled to
A party on a 70 m rope arrived at this anchor with only a couple of metres of rope left; a 60 m barely reaches

5.station: Continues down the gully. The final station sits on a rock directly below the end of the blue-green gully.
hazards: Parties report not seeing this anchor until they are on it, so do not assume you have missed it and keep going
The gully is loaded with loose rock and dirt - one party was showered with gravel while rappelling and pulling, and reported dodging larger blocks
5.pull: The route description warns specifically to take care pulling ropes in the gully because of the volume of loose rock; stand out of the fall line and expect debris to come with the rope.

6.station: The last station is at the end of the gully, on the climber's right. This rappel trends LEFT, following water-cleaned rock out of the gully to the ground, landing at a steep trail that returns to the start of the climb in a few minutes.
hazards: A 60 m only just reaches on the last two rappels of this sequence
Loose rock in the gully above continues to be the hazard until you are out of the fall line

set.rappel_count_note: Six rappels: one down the climbing line to where the descent diverges, then five on a dedicated rappel route to the ground. A single 60 m rope does the whole thing PROVIDED you use every anchor station - the route page states plainly that below the divergence you must not skip anchors or try to link rappels on a 60 or a 70, and parties confirm the last two are only just within reach of a 60. A 70 m buys exactly one thing: it links the top two rappels into a single rope-stretching 35 m shot and skips a semi-hanging belay. It does not let you skip anything lower. Note a numbering discrepancy that is not a disagreement about the route: the current route page puts the divergence at the bottom of pitch 8 while older text and every trip report say the bottom of pitch 6 - the same spot, counted with and without the traverse pitches. A walk-off exists from the top of pitch 4 by way of a fixed line, but is not recommended in climbing shoes.

1.station: The top station is a BOLTED anchor sitting roughly 20-30 ft above the old slung-block anchor at the top of pitch 6 - the old block is the landmark, the bolts are above it. Parties who do not want the full-length first rappel start instead from partway through the 4th-class scrambling on pitch 7.
hazards: Rope choice is decided at this station and the margin is not discretionary: from the top anchor two 70 m ropes reach the bolted anchor atop pitch 5, and doubled 60 m ropes DO NOT reach between them
The older slung-block anchor below the bolts is still the more obvious thing to see; it is not the current station
1.pull: On two 70s this is close to a full-length rappel, so set the knot well clear of the lip and knot the ends.

2.station: The bolted anchor at the top of pitch 5, immediately above the route's very thin slab crux. This is the station the first rappel is measured to, and the reason two 70 m ropes are the published requirement.
hazards: Slab above and below with little to stand on, so arrive at the anchor rather than near it - there is nothing to grab if you end up off line

6.station: Last rappel, down pitch 1 to the base of the wall.
hazards: Pitch 1 is described as sustained, heady and delicate with alpine crumbliness - the loosest ground on the route, and both strands run over it

set.rappel_count_note: No source publishes a rappel total for this route, and the count moves with where you start. What IS published is the rope requirement, and it is not a preference: the top station is a bolted anchor about 20-30 ft above the old pitch-6 slung-block anchor, and from it TWO 70 m ropes reach the bolted anchor atop pitch 5 while doubled 60 m ropes do not reach between those anchors. A 70 m lead rope plus a 70 m tagline is the stated ideal because it preserves the option of rappelling from the very top; a party on 60s must start lower, from partway through the 4th-class scrambling on pitch 7. Most parties do not rappel at all - they top out on the East Shoulder and take the walk-off, a very exposed and sketchy 4th-class traverse west into the descent gully, which most keep the rope on for despite poor protection. Per-station distances below the first rappel are not published; the uniform 70 m figures on file are the rope's capacity rather than measurements, and six 70 m rappels would be far more than the height of the route.

1.station: The summit anchor - the heavily slung summit boulder - dropping down the upper north face to what published accounts call the only bolted anchor on the whole rappel route. Everything below it is slung natural gear, so this is the one station you can identify with certainty.
hazards: A single 60 m rope does NOT reach the bolts: you finish roughly 10 ft above them and downclimb easy 5th class to get there. A 70 m single is the length that reaches, and is what recent parties recommend
This is the rappel where a party got a rope end stuck in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 back up to free it
1.pull: Keep both ends clear of the constriction above the wide crack before the last climber pulls - it is the documented rope trap on this descent.

2.station: Down toward the main ledge system. Parties on two ropes report doubling up and rappelling climber's-LEFT of the climbing line to reach the next station rather than dropping straight down it.
hazards: The line does not follow the route, so what you see going down is not what you climbed

3.station: A single rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.
hazards: Ledge-to-ledge rappelling on this face means loose material sitting on every stance above you

4.station: From the ledge, cut climber's LEFT to the station, which sits just after you walk back underneath the large block. Published accounts also describe a station at the top of pitch 4 reached by a ledge traverse - the ledge is the feature to navigate by, not the fall line.
hazards: You have to walk under and past a large block to find this station, so it is not visible from where the previous rappel lands
Traversing a ledge with the ropes still out is where they snag on this descent

5.station: The last rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col. From the final stance the rappel route is a straight shot through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.
hazards: The notch is the aiming point; below the col the descent continues down loose gullies on foot

set.rappel_count_note: The five stations on file are the DOUBLE-ROPE count. The same descent is not five rappels for everyone: a party taking many shorter rappels on a single rope logged 9-10 to reverse the route back to Burgundy Col, and a party on two 60 m ropes describes doubling up for the first, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to the col. Neither is wrong. Action Potential has no rappel line of its own - parties finish into North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge and take that route's descent. On rope choice the published accounts disagree in a way worth knowing: two ropes are faster, but one first-hand account calls double ropes on this descent annoying and prone to getting stuck, and recommends a single 70 m instead - a single 60 m leaves you about 10 ft above the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not published in any account read for this entry; the figures on file come from the route's own descent text rather than from measurement.

1.station: The slung summit boulder, dropping down the upper north face to the only bolted anchor anywhere on this rappel route. Below it every station is slung natural gear, so this is the single anchor you can positively identify.
hazards: A single 60 m rope comes up about 10 ft short of the bolts and the last of it is an unroped downclimb on easy 5th class; a 70 m single reaches
A party rappelling here got a rope end wedged in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 to recover it
1.pull: The constriction above the wide crack is the documented rope-eater on this face. Watch where the ends land and keep both strands out of it.

2.station: Down toward the main ledge system, rappelling climber's-LEFT of the climbing line rather than straight down it.
hazards: The rappel line diverges from the climb, so the terrain below you is ground you have not seen

3.station: One rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.
hazards: Loose material accumulates on these ledges and sits directly above whoever is next on the rope

4.station: Cut climber's LEFT from the ledge; the station is just past the point where you walk back underneath the large block. Accounts also describe a station at the top of pitch 4 reached by traversing the ledge - navigate by the ledge and the block, not by looking straight down.
hazards: Not visible from where the previous rappel lands - you have to walk under the block to find it
Traversing with ropes deployed is where they hang up here

5.station: The remaining rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col; from the last stance the line is a straight shot down through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.
hazards: Below the col the descent is loose gullies on foot rather than more rappelling

set.rappel_count_note: Five stations is the DOUBLE-ROPE count. Ultramega OK has no rappel line of its own - it is a Northeast Buttress route that merges into upper North Face terrain, and parties take the North Face descent. The same ground is 9-10 rappels for a party doing many shorter ones on a single rope, and a two-60 party describes it as a doubled first rappel, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to Burgundy Col - all three counts describe one descent under different rope setups. Rope opinion is genuinely split rather than settled: two ropes are quicker, but a first-hand account calls double ropes here annoying and prone to sticking and prefers a single 70 m, and a single 60 m does not reach the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not published in any account read for this entry.

1.station: The rappel line starts down and SKIER'S LEFT of the summit, not on it. The top station is a bolted anchor - reached, from the West Face finish, by continuing about 50 ft above the top of that route's last pitch. It is worth noting where this anchor is on the way up: parties descending at dusk say knowing where the first anchors are is what makes a late descent reasonable. First of three single-rope rappels heading down toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: Rope drag and route-finding after the slab traverse make this a confusing place to arrive; the anchor is above where most parties stop
The descent is repeatedly described as windy, which throws a tossed rope off line

2.station: Second of the three single-rope rappels, down into the gully.
hazards: This is the rappel reported as coming up about 5 ft short on a 60 m rope, finished with a short downclimb. Expect it rather than discovering it at the ends
The gully is loose and chossy, and snow-covered well into the season

3.station: Third single-rope rappel, landing in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire - often snow-covered. There is a tree at the notch that parties use as the landmark for the anchors here. A few minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing links this to the chockstone station.
hazards: The gully here is the one parties mistakenly ASCEND when route-finding up the chasm; on the way down it is loose and often snow-filled
Rockfall onto anyone still on the rappel above

4.station: The rappel this descent is known for. Below the notch, a short scramble leads to the giant chockstone in the gully; the station is a BOLTED rap anchor on top of the chockstone - not tat, and the same bolts parties belay from on the way up when climbing the Chockstone Route. The rappel goes off the chockstone and hangs completely free for around 50 ft, and is routinely described as the longest free-hanging rappel the party has done.
hazards: Fully free-hanging with no way to reach rock once you are on it
You arrive at this station from above by scrambling loose gully ground, which is where material gets knocked onto anyone below

5.station: A few more minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing below the chockstone, then a last short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree to the ground. Some parties downclimb this instead of rigging it.
hazards: Loose, steep gully walking either way

set.rappel_count_note: These five stations are the ORIGINAL chockstone/notch descent down the south side, and the count assumes a SINGLE rope for the three upper rappels plus TWO ropes for the chockstone rappel - sources describe it as up to five rappels depending on conditions and the number of ropes carried, and parties with two ropes throughout combine some of the upper ones. The second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m. IMPORTANT: this is probably not the descent a Labor Pains party will use. A separate BOLTED rappel line was established down the West Face, running between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, and Labor Pains' own published gear note calls for a 70 m rope specifically to take advantage of those West Face rappels. That line shares only the FIRST anchor with the chockstone descent - from it you head down the West Face instead of into the gully - and has nothing else in common with the stations listed here. It is currently six stations on bolts and chains ending a minute from the base of the routes, with one rappel that a 60 m does not make (parties report needing to block and extend a strand, or carry a 70), and a last anchor that is genuinely hard to find, on a rib below some shrubs and skier's left as you walk down loose dirt from the fifth station. Some parties still rappel from a nearby dead tree carrying no slings, which is not the anchor. Do not blend the two lines: the station list on file is the chockstone line.

1.station: The rappels begin at M&M Ledge. From it, work climber's LEFT to reach good bolts - the bolted stations are not directly beneath where the ledge drops you, and finding them is the only route-finding on this descent. If you rappel from the ledge's own anchor instead, that is a fixed piton and a fixed wire, and the rappel from it also trends climber's left.
hazards: The M&M Ledge anchor is two pieces of old fixed gear, a pin and a wire. A large and reportedly bomber horn sits up and left of it that would make a much better station and nobody has rigged it - carry cord if you want to use it
Because the line trends left rather than dropping straight down, a rope end blown or thrown off line is awkward to recover

2.station: Second station on the bolted line down the East Face.
hazards: Steep sustained face with nothing to stand on between stations - once on the rope you are committed to reaching the next anchor

3.station: Third station on the bolted line.
hazards: Anything knocked off a station here falls the full height of the wall

4.station: Last rappel, essentially reaching the ground at the base of the East Face - the side you approached from, so this is where your pack is.
hazards: Talus and snow at the base of the face for much of the season

set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels off bolts, reached by working climber's LEFT from M&M Ledge, and the description that gives that sequence assumes TWO ropes - four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground. Parties who first rappel from M&M Ledge's own fixed pin-and-wire anchor, which also trends climber's left, count five. No single-rope option is described for this line. The alternative descent, for parties who continue to the true summit rather than rappelling from the ledge, is the standard Liberty Bell notch route - a downclimb east to a two-bolt station and two rappels of about 25 m into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch - which is fewer rappels but lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face approach and from your pack. Per-station distances are not published; the figures on file assume near-full-length double-rope rappels.

1.station: A small step down from the summit leads to the notch where the easy version of pitch 4 ends, and the tree growing there is the top anchor. As of a 2021 inventory it carries three rap rings plus a quantity of slings and cord. About 25 m back down to the pitch-3 ledge.
hazards: Large clefts flank the line that look purpose-built to catch a rope - feed the rope down rather than throwing it
Trip reports repeatedly record the rope sticking on this descent and needing tugging to free
1.pull: Decide which side you are pulling from before the last climber leaves, and keep both strands clear of the clefts.

2.station: The station on the pitch-3 ledge, where the first rappel lands. Currently an 8 mm cordelette doubled around the anchor with two quicklinks.
hazards: A 60 m rope doubled comes up just slightly short of the tree at the top of pitch 2, so the last few metres are an unroped downscramble. An added pitch-3 anchor exists specifically to cut that exposure out on a 60 m

3.station: The ledge at the top of pitch 2: the anchor is the large, straight tree on the skier's-LEFT side. Two trees here each carry a few slings, and by August 2024 a rock-based anchor had been added alongside them.
hazards: The tree has taken most of the traffic on this peak for years and its long-term health is a stated concern - use the rock anchor beside it where it is in place
The lower rappels are lichen-covered and slippery when wet
3.pull: The tree sits back from the lip, so the rope saws across the flat top of the ledge and this pull is stiff. Pull from immediately beside the slung rock horn at the top of pitch 1 - moving any further out before pulling is what jams it.

4.station: Atop pitch 1, a block and horn carrying several slings and three rap rings - the same spot you pull the previous rope from. About 30 m returns you to exactly where you first roped up.
hazards: A slung block rather than fixed hardware: load it in line with the pull rather than shifting it

A second, partly hidden set of bolts sits off to the side of pitches 1 and 2 so descending parties do not have to share ground with climbers. It is a different line, and it needs a small swing climber's-right at the bottom to put your feet on the ground; continuing along the ramp there creates rope drag that makes the pull difficult

set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a SINGLE 60 m rope used doubled, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches back to Pineapple Pass - this is what almost every party does and how the stations are spaced. Two 60 m ropes let you link them into fewer, longer rappels. One 60 m rappel in the sequence comes up just short of the next tree, leaving a short unroped downscramble, which an added pitch-3 anchor now avoids. A separate, partly hidden bolted line beside pitches 1 and 2 exists so that ascending and descending parties are not in the same place; it is a different set of anchors, not a variation. Below Pineapple Pass the east gully holds two more bolted chain stations for two further rappels on a 60 m - optional, and many parties scramble out instead; there is meaningful rockfall hazard in that gully. Do not scramble directly up to Pineapple Pass on the way in: that ground is the rappel route.
